subject: korean
title: One idiom, two feelings
goal: Infer the shared figurative meaning of 손이 크다 from three sentences, decide where it carries a complaint, and explain with quoted evidence why the feeling differs.
thinking: Inferring an idiom's meaning from several contexts
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks which meaning a listed idiom has. Here the idiom is never glossed: you infer it from three uses and then judge why the same words sound warm in one sentence and worrying in another.
prerequisites: Can read Korean sentences with -아서/-어서 and -(으)ㄹ 때마다
Knows that Korean has fixed expressions whose meaning is not the sum of their words
material:
Three people talk about someone. The same expression 손이 크다 appears each time (it is NOT glossed here).
(가) 엄마는 손이 커서 김장할 때마다 이웃 몫까지 넉넉하게 담그세요.
(나) 동생은 손이 커서 월급날이면 친구들에게 밥을 사다가 월말에는 늘 빠듯해요.
(다) 새 요리사는 손이 커서 찌개를 끓이면 늘 열 명 분이 나와서 매번 반이 남아요.

steps.prompt: Which core meaning of 손이 크다 fits all three sentences?
hints: Cover the idiom and ask what the three situations (김장, 월급날, 찌개) have in common.
Test each option against all three sentences, not only the one that sounds easiest.

options.text: The person has physically large hands that are useful in the kitchen.
options.reveals: Taking the words literally. Check (나): a paycheck and treating friends have nothing to do with hand size.

options.text: The person is a skilled cook who makes tasty food in any situation.
options.reveals: Anchoring on (가) and (다). Check (나): there is no cooking in it, so the meaning must be wider than cooking.

options.text: The person spends money without thinking about tomorrow.
options.reveals: Fits (나) only. Check (가) and (다): they are about the amount of food, not about careless spending.

options.text: The person handles food, money or gifts in large, generous amounts.
options.reveals: Building a meaning that survives all three contexts, not just the first one.

steps.explain: In all three, 손이 크다 describes someone who uses, gives or makes things in big quantities. Cooking and money are only the settings.

steps.prompt: In which sentences does the speaker treat 손이 크다 as at least a mild problem? Choose all that apply.
hints: For each sentence, ask how the speaker sounds: pleased, neutral or worried?
Then find the words in the sentence that make you feel that.

options.text: (가) 엄마 ... 이웃 몫까지 넉넉하게 담그세요
options.reveals: Reading 넉넉하게 / 이웃 몫까지 as a warm detail, not a complaint. The sentence has no negative result.

options.text: (나) 동생 ... 월말에는 늘 빠듯해요
options.reveals: Noticing the result clause 빠듯해요 (money is tight) turns the same habit into a worry.

options.text: (다) 새 요리사 ... 매번 반이 남아요
options.reveals: Noticing 매번 반이 남아요 (half is wasted every time) as the negative result.

steps.explain: The idiom's core meaning is neutral. The feeling comes from the result clause: 빠듯해요 and 반이 남아요 signal a problem, while 넉넉하게 in (가) is friendly.

steps.prompt: In English or Korean, explain why the same idiom feels warm in (가) but worrying in (나). Quote at least one Korean phrase from the sentences as evidence.
hints: Quote the result clause of each sentence.
State what is the same (the idiom) and what is different (the outcome).

checks.label: quotes Korean evidence from the sentences
links the feeling to the context or result

selfAssess: Did I say what stays the same and what changes?
Did I point to the exact words that carry the feeling?
Could a classmate find my evidence in the text?

modelAnswers.text: In (가) the clause 이웃 몫까지 넉넉하게 shows sharing, so being generous is praised. In (나) the same habit leads to 월말에는 늘 빠듯해요, so the outcome is a money problem. The idiom is the same; the result clause changes the feeling.
손이 크다 only says that she or he uses things in large amounts. In (가) that helps the neighbours, but in (나) 빠듯해요 shows it costs the brother money, so the speaker sounds worried.
(가) 넉넉하게 담그세요 is a gift to the neighbours so it feels warm; (나) 월말에는 늘 빠듯해요 is a money problem so it feels worrying.

badAnswers.text: It means that the person has big hands, so it is warm.
badAnswers.why: No Korean evidence and a literal reading of the idiom.

badAnswers.text: It means big hands, but 김장 is warm
badAnswers.why: Quotes a Korean word but gives no link between the result and the feeling, and reads the idiom literally.

steps.humanReview: Whether the quoted phrase really supports the claimed feeling, and whether the learner treats connotation as coming from context.

rubric.full: States a meaning that fits all three sentences (generous/large amounts)
rubric.partial: Fits only cooking or only money

rubric.full: Quotes the result clauses and links them to the feeling

alternatives: Answers that call the core meaning 'spending freely' or 'making much' are both acceptable if they cover 김장 and 월급날.
A learner may say (다) is neutral; accept if 반이 남아요 is discussed.
hardCases: Some speakers use 손이 크다 as praise for generosity even when money gets tight; the judgement in s2 depends on the result clause, not on the idiom.

cautions.language: Idioms are shown unglossed on purpose; the options give English paraphrases only.
cautions.culture: Kimchi-making (김장) and treating friends on payday are common Korean settings; the task does not assume every learner knows them, since the sentences explain the result.
cautions.accessibility: No images. Text is plain; the numbered (가)(나)(다) labels are read aloud by screen readers as gana, nada, dada: say 'sentence one, two, three' if needed.

auto: Choices in s1 and s2 against the key
Presence of quoted Korean and a context word in s3
human: Whether the explanation actually connects the result clause with the feeling

subject: korean
title: Reading a headline against its numbers
goal: Find the sentence in a short news article that claims more than the evidence supports, and rewrite the headline so that it matches the data and notes a limit of the survey.
thinking: Checking a claim against the numbers
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks the meaning of news vocabulary such as 과반 or 응답자. Here you must use those words to test whether a conclusion follows from the numbers and then write a corrected headline.
prerequisites: Can read percentages and numbers in Korean news
Knows the words 찬성, 반대, 응답자
Knows 다수 (many / most) and 과반 (more than half)
material:
Headline: 서울 시민 다수, 대중교통 요금 인상 찬성
(Read the headline first, then the four sentences of the article, numbered 1 to 4.)

steps.prompt: One sentence claims more than the sentences before it support. Which one?
hints: Compare the percentages in the second sentence with the conclusion drawn in the last one.
Ask who the 1,000 people actually were before deciding what they can speak for.
lines: 서울시가 시민 1,000명에게 대중교통 요금 인상에 대한 의견을 물었다.
조사는 평일 출근 시간대 지하철역 앞에서 만난 시민만을 대상으로 했다.
이에 따라 서울 시민 다수가 요금 인상을 지지하는 것으로 나타났다.
steps.explain: Line 4 is the overreach. 다수 sounds like 'most', but 48% is less than half and 41% opposed: 찬성 is the largest group (a plurality), not a majority. Line 3 also shows that only people met at subway stations at rush hour answered, so they cannot speak for all Seoul citizens.

steps.prompt: Rewrite the headline in Korean so that it matches the numbers, and add one sentence (Korean or English) that names a limit of this survey.
hints: Use the actual figures from line 2 instead of a vague word.
Look at line 3 for the limit.

checks.label: uses a figure from line 2 (48 or 41)
does not claim that a majority supports the increase
names a limit of the sample

selfAssess: Does my headline say only what 48% and 41% allow?
Is the limit I named about who was asked, not about the topic?
Would a reader of my headline be misled about 'all citizens'?

modelAnswers.text: 서울 시민 48% 요금 인상 찬성…반대 41%로 과반엔 못 미쳐. (조사는 출근 시간대 지하철역 앞 시민만 대상이라 전체 시민의 의견으로 보기 어렵다.)
요금 인상 찬성 48%, 반대 41%… 찬성이 가장 많지만 절반은 안 돼. 조사 대상이 출근길 지하철역 이용자뿐이라는 한계가 있다.
찬성 48%, 반대 41%… 찬성이 가장 많지만 과반은 아니다. 평일 아침에 만난 사람만 물었다는 한계가 있다.

badAnswers.text: 서울 시민 다수가 요금 인상에 찬성
badAnswers.why: Keeps the unsupported claim and gives no figure or limit.

badAnswers.text: 서울 시민 절반 요금 인상 찬성, 48%
badAnswers.why: Uses the figure but ignores the sampling limit.
Uses the figure and mentions who was asked, but names no limit of the sample.

steps.humanReview: Whether the rewritten headline is natural headline style and whether the limit named is really about representativeness.

rubric.full: Rewrite uses the figures and avoids 'majority'
rubric.partial: Uses figures but still implies most citizens agree

rubric.full: Names who was asked and why that limits the conclusion

alternatives: A headline such as '찬성 48%·반대 41%…엇갈린 시민 의견' is also good.
Pointing out that 11% had no opinion is a valid extra remark.
hardCases: Some may argue 48% is 'about half' and the headline 절반 would be fine; the sampling limit still stops 'Seoul citizens' generalisations.

cautions.language: Newspaper headline style drops endings and uses '…' and '·'; model answers imitate this, but plain sentences are accepted.
cautions.culture: The survey is invented and no real organisation is meant; 서울시 appears only as a setting.
cautions.accessibility: No images. Percent signs are read as 'percent' by most screen readers; the numbers are also spelled in the explanation.

auto: Position of the unsupported line
Presence of the figure, absence of a majority claim, and a sample-limit word
human: Naturalness of the headline and quality of the stated limit

subject: korean
title: Does the library cause the grades?
goal: Decide which additional information would help test whether library use causes higher grades, spot a reversed-cause reading, and write one question for the researcher.
thinking: Choosing the information that would settle a claim
differsFromPlain: Plain practice reads a news article for its main idea. Here you ask what the article does not tell you and which missing facts would change your judgement.
prerequisites: Can read a short Korean news summary
Knows the words 성적, 이용, 평균
material: News summary: 한 연구에서 한 달에 도서관을 8번 이상 이용한 학생의 평균 성적이 2번 미만 이용한 학생보다 높았다. 연구자는 "도서관 이용이 성적을 올린다"고 말했다.

steps.prompt: Which extra facts would help you decide whether library use CAUSES higher grades? Choose all that apply.
hints: For each option ask: would the answer change how likely it is that the library is the cause?
Ask what else could differ between frequent and rare library users.

options.text: Whether the same students' grades were measured before and after they began to use the library often
options.reveals: Looking for change over time in the same people, which a single comparison cannot show.

options.text: Which kinds of books the students borrowed most often
options.reveals: An interesting detail about use, but it does not tell you whether the use or something else produces the grades.

options.text: Whether students who use the library a lot already study more or are more motivated
options.reveals: Looking for a third factor that could explain both library use and grades.

options.text: What the average grade of all students in the country is
options.reveals: A national average shows whether these students are typical, not what causes their gap.

options.text: Whether grades came from school records or from the students' own reports
options.reveals: Checking how reliable the grade numbers are; this helps the whole claim, though it is not about cause itself.

steps.explain: To test cause you need before/after data on the same students (a) and a check of other factors such as study time or motivation (c). Book types and a national average do not bear on the cause.

acceptable.reason: Checking how grades were measured (e) is reasonable because it tests the reliability of the data, even though it does not directly address cause.

steps.prompt: A reader says: "Maybe students with high grades like studying, so they go to the library more." Which idea does this show?
hints: Compare what the study says with what the reader says: in each, which is the cause and which is the effect?
Check which option is about direction, not honesty or sampling.

options.text: The study must have been dishonest.
options.reveals: Jumping to accusing the study; the reader's idea is about direction, not honesty.

options.text: Library use and grades are certainly unrelated.
options.reveals: Overcorrecting: reversing the direction does not mean there is no link.

options.text: The cause may run the other way: high grades (or studious habits) may lead to more library use.
options.reveals: Considering the reverse direction of cause and effect.

options.text: Only students who like reading were surveyed.
options.reveals: Mixing in a sampling worry that the reader's sentence does not mention.

steps.explain: The reader proposes reverse causation. The same numbers fit both directions, which is why the claim that library use raises grades goes beyond the data.

steps.prompt: In Korean, write ONE question you would ask the researcher before accepting "도서관 이용이 성적을 올린다".
hints: Choose a missing fact from step 1, or the reverse direction from step 2.
Think what you would need to know in order to rule out another explanation.

checks.label: is phrased as a question
asks about change over time, other factors, the direction of cause, or how grades were measured

selfAssess: Does my question point to a missing fact, not just doubt?
Could the answer change my judgement?

modelAnswers.text: 도서관을 자주 이용하기 전에는 같은 학생들의 성적이 어땠나요?
도서관을 자주 가는 학생들이 원래 공부를 더 열심히 하는 학생은 아닌가요?
성적이 높은 학생이 도서관에 더 자주 가는 것은 아닐까요?
학생들의 성적은 학교 기록에서 가져왔나요?

badAnswers.why: A question, but about nothing specific.
A statement, not a question.

badAnswers.text: 도서관 때문에 성적이 오르는 게 맞나요?
badAnswers.why: A question, but it only repeats the claim and asks for no missing fact.

steps.humanReview: Whether the question is natural and genuinely probes cause.

rubric.full: Picks before/after data and other factors and rejects fame/brand
A specific question that could change the judgement
rubric.partial: Specific topic but not a question

alternatives: Option e can be chosen with a and c.
Questions in English are not accepted for s3 on purpose; the aim is to produce Korean.
hardCases: A student may say sample size is the missing fact; this is relevant but is not in the options, so it is a good extra in s3.

cautions.language: The summary uses '때문에', the key cause marker, on purpose; the task points at this word.
cautions.culture: Phones and school grades are common concerns, no real study or person is named.
cautions.accessibility: No images. Numbers are written out in words (four hours, two hours) in the model answers where needed.

auto: Choices in s1 and s2
Question form and keyword presence in s3

subject: korean
title: Reading 'oh, okay…'
goal: Revise your reading of a coworker's reply as more of the chat is revealed, and explain which Korean phrases changed your mind.
thinking: Revising a judgement with new evidence
differsFromPlain: Plain practice translates short chat lines. Here the same few words are reread three times as more context arrives, and you track how and why your interpretation changes.
prerequisites: Can read casual Korean chat
Knows that 괜찮아 and 알겠습니다 can be said without agreeing happily
Knows 막내 (the youngest member) and 어차피 (anyway)
material: A team chat at a Korean company. 지민 is the newest member. 선배 is a senior colleague. The chat is revealed in three steps.

steps.prompt: Read each piece of the chat. After each, pick the most reasonable reading of what 지민 feels.
hints: Ask yourself what is said and what is only implied.
After each new piece, check whether your earlier reading still fits.

stages.info:
선배: 내일 회의 자료, 누가 정리해 줄 수 있을까?
지민: 아, 네…
stages.ask: What does '아, 네…' most likely signal?

options.text: She is glad to volunteer.
options.reveals: Reading 네 as enthusiasm and ignoring the trailing '아' and '…'.

options.text: She heard the question and is hesitating, without clearly volunteering.
options.reveals: Noticing that 네 here answers 'I hear you', not 'I will do it'.

options.text: She clearly refuses.
options.reveals: Reading refusal into a word that literally means yes.

stages.after: At this point only a hesitation is visible. 네 can mean 'I heard you', and the opening '아' and the ending '…' suggest unease.

stages.info:
선배: 그럼 지민 씨가 해 줄래요?
지민: 제가요? 아… 네, 알겠습니다.
stages.ask: How should you now read her answer?

options.text: She will do it but is not happy about it.
options.reveals: Seeing that '알겠습니다' is compliance while '제가요?' shows surprise.

options.text: She is delighted and thanking the senior.
options.reveals: Treating the formal 알겠습니다 as warmth.

options.text: She said no politely.
options.reveals: Missing that 알겠습니다 is an acceptance.

stages.after: 알겠습니다 accepts the job, while 제가요? and the pause show surprise and reluctance. She complied; that is different from agreeing gladly.

stages.info: Later, 지민 writes to a friend: "자료 정리? 뭐, 어차피 내가 제일 막내인데 어쩌겠어. 괜찮아."
stages.ask: Suppose the senior learned what she wrote to her friend. What is the best next step?

options.text: Thank her warmly in the team chat and leave it there.
options.reveals: Kind, but it answers 'she is fine' and ignores the one-sided burden she describes with 어쩌겠어.

options.text: Offer to share the task or help, and check in with her.
options.reveals: Treating 어쩌겠어 and 막내 as signals of a one-sided burden.

options.text: Say nothing, because she accepted.
options.reveals: Equating acceptance with agreement.

stages.after: 어쩌겠어 means she saw no real choice, and 막내 explains why. 괜찮아 here sounds like a way to close the topic, not a statement of comfort.

steps.reflect: The same words, 네 and 괜찮아, had different weight each time. Pausing marks like 아… and phrases like 어쩌겠어 carry what the polite words do not say.

steps.prompt: In English or Korean, explain how your reading changed from the first to the last piece. Quote at least two Korean phrases that moved you.
hints: Name the first reading you had, then the phrase that made you revise it.
Pick phrases from different pieces of the chat.

checks.label: quotes at least TWO different Korean phrases from the chat
describes a change of reading

selfAssess: Did I say what I first thought?
Did I tie the change to specific phrases?

modelAnswers.text: At first I read '아, 네…' as a plain yes, but '제가요?' showed surprise and reluctance, and later '어쩌겠어' told me she accepted only because she is the youngest. So '괜찮아' does not mean she is fine.
My view changed after 제가요? and 어쩌겠어. Polite words like 알겠습니다 hid how she felt, and at the end 괜찮아 was her way to end the topic.

badAnswers.why: No quoted Korean and no change of reading.
Quotes only one phrase and shows no change of reading.

steps.humanReview: Whether the quoted phrases truly drive the revised reading.

rubric.full: Describes first reading, the trigger phrase, and the new reading
rubric.partial: Describes a change without naming a trigger

rubric.full: Quotes phrases from at least two pieces

alternatives: In stage 1, 'she has not decided yet' is also reasonable; the key is not reading it as enthusiasm.
In stage 3 a student may argue for gently asking 지민 first; this counts as option b.
hardCases: Some readers hear 괜찮아 as genuinely fine. The task asks for the best-supported reading, not certainty.

cautions.language: Ellipsis marks (…) in chat carry tone; they are read as 'dot dot dot' by screen readers, so the stage text mentions the pause in words.
cautions.culture: Hierarchy by age or rank (막내 = the youngest member) is typical of many Korean workplaces; not every workplace works this way.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The chat is plain text with speaker names.

auto: Choices in the reveal stages
Quoted phrases and a change word in s2

subject: korean
title: Late homework, polite message
goal: Judge what is off in a text to a professor, then rewrite it so that it asks permission, identifies the writer, and gives a reason.
thinking: Evaluating a message for its audience
differsFromPlain: Plain practice conjugates -습니다/-어요 endings. Here you decide which features of a real message misfire with a professor and then rewrite the whole message, not a single ending.
prerequisites: Can write -습니다 and -(으)ㄹ까요 sentences
Knows the words 교수님, 과제, 제출
material:
A student sends this KakaoTalk message to a professor at 11 p.m. (ㅎㅎ is a chat abbreviation for laughing, said 'hieut hieut'; ~ is a tilde that adds a light, friendly tone.)

"교수님 과제 내일 낼게요 ㅎㅎ 몸이 좀 안 좋아서요. 확인 부탁해요~"

steps.prompt: Which features of this message would a Korean professor probably find inappropriate? Choose all that apply.
hints: Imagine you are the professor reading it at 11 p.m. What would you need to know?
Separate what the message fails to DO (ask, identify the writer) from how it merely SOUNDS.

options.text: It announces the new deadline ('낼게요') instead of asking permission
options.reveals: Seeing that the writer is deciding something that belongs to the professor.

options.text: The laughing abbreviation and the tilde make the tone casual
options.reveals: Noticing register markers that suit friends more than a professor.

options.text: The writer does not say who they are or which class they attend
options.reveals: Seeing that the professor may teach many students and cannot tell who writes.

options.text: The message gives illness as the reason for the delay
options.reveals: Treating a reason as a fault, although a reason is exactly what is expected.

options.text: It uses the -요 ending rather than the more formal -습니다
options.reveals: Judging endings: -요 is polite; a formal ending is a plus, but not the main fault here.

steps.explain: The core problems are that the writer announces rather than asks (a) and does not identify themselves (c). The casual markers (b) and the -요 ending (e) are debatable, and giving a reason (d) is good practice.

acceptable.reason: Many readers also find the symbols too casual for a professor; this is a reasonable extra.
A more formal ending is expected in a written message to a professor, so noticing it is reasonable.
Noticing both the casual markers and the ending, besides the two core problems, is a reasonable extra.

steps.prompt: Rewrite the message in Korean (2-4 sentences) for the professor. Keep the reason, ask for permission, and say who you are.
hints: Start with a greeting and your name or class.
Turn the deadline into a question.

checks.label: opens with a greeting
asks permission or makes a request
keeps a reason
avoids casual markers and announcing
says who the writer is (name or class)

selfAssess: Does the professor know who I am?
Did I ask rather than tell?
Is the whole message in one respectful register?

modelAnswers.text: 교수님, 안녕하세요. 한국어문학과 수업을 듣는 이서연입니다. 어제부터 몸이 좋지 않아 과제를 오늘까지 제출하기 어려울 것 같습니다. 내일까지 제출해도 괜찮을까요? 양해해 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
안녕하세요, 교수님. 목요일 3교시 수업의 김민준입니다. 감기 몸살로 과제를 마무리하지 못했습니다. 하루만 늦게 제출할 수 있을까요? 죄송하지만 허락해 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
교수님, 안녕하세요. 월요일 수업 박서연입니다. 건강이 안 좋아 과제를 하루 늦게 제출해도 되는지 여쭙고 싶습니다.
안녕하세요, 교수님. 화요일 수업의 최민호입니다. 몸이 아파서 과제를 내일 제출해도 되겠습니까? 죄송합니다.

badAnswers.text: 교수님 과제 내일 낼게요 ㅎㅎ 몸이 안 좋아서요
badAnswers.why: The original message: casual, announces, no greeting.

badAnswers.text: 안녕하세요 교수님. 몸이 안 좋아서 과제는 내일 낼게요.
badAnswers.why: Has a greeting and a reason but still announces and does not ask or identify the writer.

steps.humanReview: Whether the register is consistent and the message sounds natural.

rubric.full: Greets, identifies, gives reason, asks permission
Consistently formal (-습니다/-ㄹ까요), no casual symbols

alternatives: Using -요 endings can be accepted if the other functions are present.
A message that offers a make-up plan (e.g. emailing a draft today) is an excellent extra.
hardCases: Whether to add an apology word varies; both a short 죄송합니다 and none can be fine.

cautions.language: Written messages to professors usually take -습니다/-ㄹ까요 endings; -요 is also widely used, so the checker does not demand a particular ending.
cautions.culture: Norms about messaging a professor late at night differ between universities; many students send such messages the next morning.
cautions.accessibility: No images. ㅎㅎ and ~ are explained in words so that a screen reader's reading is not required to understand them.

auto: Choices in s1
Greeting, request, reason and absence of casual markers in s2
human: Naturalness and register of the rewrite

subject: korean
title: The idiom that contradicts its sentence
goal: Find the sentence where an idiom clashes with the rest of the sentence, choose a repair, and then repair a second clashing sentence yourself.
thinking: Detecting a contradiction between an idiom and its context
Making an idiom and its context agree
differsFromPlain: Plain practice matches idioms to meanings. Here the meanings are not asked; you detect which use fails and why, and then repair a second clashing sentence.
prerequisites: Knows the idioms 발등에 불이 떨어지다, 누워서 떡 먹기, 발이 넓다 as vocabulary items
Can read short learner essays
material: A learner wrote four sentences for a class blog and used an idiom in each. (Idioms: 발등에 불이 떨어지다 = to face an urgent problem; 누워서 떡 먹기 = to be very easy; 발이 넓다 = to know many people; 소문난 잔치에 먹을 것 없다 = hype that exceeds the reality.)

steps.prompt: One sentence uses an idiom in a way that contradicts the rest of the sentence. Which line?
hints: Replace the idiom in each line with its meaning, then reread.
Look for a result that does not follow from the idiom.
lines: 발표 전날 밤에 자료가 사라져서 정말 발등에 불이 떨어졌어요.
큰일인 줄 알았는데 막상 해 보니 누워서 떡 먹기였어요.
우리 팀장님은 발이 넓어서 하루도 모임에 가지 않고 집에만 계세요.
소문난 잔치에 먹을 것 없다더니 그 식당이 딱 그랬어요.
steps.explain: Line 3 is the problem. 발이 넓다 means to know many people, but the rest says the team leader stays home and goes to no gatherings. The other three idioms fit their contexts.

steps.prompt: Which repair of line 3 keeps the idiom and makes the sentence logical?
hints: Ask which options still make sense if 발이 넓다 means 'knows many people'.
Eliminate options that stay on the literal meaning of feet.

options.text: 우리 팀장님은 발이 넓어서 키가 큰 편이시고 신발을 따로 맞추세요.
options.reveals: Reading the idiom literally as wide feet.

options.text: 우리 팀장님은 발이 넓어서 여러 부서 사람들을 두루 아시고 소개도 잘해 주세요.
options.reveals: Keeping the idiom and giving it a result that matches 'knows many people'.

options.text: 우리 팀장님은 발이 넓어서 요즘은 사람들을 피해 집에서 쉬는 날이 많으세요.
options.reveals: Keeps the idiom, but the result still does not follow: knowing many people is not a reason to avoid people.

options.text: 우리 팀장님은 발이 넓어서 신발 가게에서 고르는 데 시간이 오래 걸려요.
options.reveals: Reading the idiom literally as wide feet and shoe shopping.

steps.explain: A good repair keeps 발이 넓다 as 'knows many people' and adds a consequence, such as knowing people across departments. Literal readings (a, d) use the words, not the idiom, and c keeps the clash.

steps.prompt: Another learner wrote: "그 식당은 소문난 잔치에 먹을 것 없다더니 음식이 정말 맛있고 줄도 길어서 매일 가요." The idiom clashes with the rest. Rewrite it as ONE Korean sentence so that the idiom (or another expression) and the rest agree, changing as little as you can.
hints: Decide what the idiom says about the restaurant, then check whether the rest of the sentence says the same thing.
You may change the rest of the sentence to match the idiom, or change the opening to match the rest.

checks.label: does not keep the idiom together with praise
has a word that agrees with the idiom or replaces it
is a complete sentence about the restaurant

selfAssess: If I kept the idiom, does the rest of my sentence say the same thing as the idiom?
Did I change only what was needed?

modelAnswers.text: 그 식당은 소문난 잔치에 먹을 것 없다더니 줄만 길고 음식은 별로여서 실망했어요.
그 식당은 소문대로 음식이 정말 맛있고 줄도 길어서 매일 가요.

badAnswers.text: 그 식당은 소문난 잔치에 먹을 것 없다더니 음식이 정말 맛있고 줄도 길어서 매일 가요.
badAnswers.why: The original sentence: the idiom still clashes with the praise.
Not a repair; says nothing about the restaurant.

steps.humanReview: Whether the repaired sentence reads naturally and the idiom and the rest of the sentence really agree.

rubric.full: Finds the line and says what clashes
rubric.partial: Finds the line without a reason

rubric.full: Sentence with idiom and a clause that fits its meaning
rubric.none: No idiom or a clashing context

alternatives: Line 2 can be argued weak if the writer found it hard; the clash in line 3 is stronger.
In s3 a learner may keep the idiom and make the rest negative, or drop the idiom and keep the praise; both repair the clash.
hardCases: Writing 소문난 잔치 together with a mixed result (long queue but bad food) is fine; check that the result is not praise only.

cautions.language: Idioms are glossed in English in the material because the aim is to judge use, not to recall meanings.
cautions.culture: Idioms like 발이 넓다 and 누워서 떡 먹기 are everyday expressions; none refer to a particular group or religion.
cautions.accessibility: No images. Idioms are written in plain Hangul.

auto: The error line in s1
The repair choice in s2
No idiom + praise clash and an agreeing word in s3
human: Whether the repaired sentence is natural and consistent

subject: korean
title: Opposed, but not 'most'
goal: Find the headline that overreaches for given poll results, then build three poll result sets for which 'more opposed than in favour' is true but 'a majority opposes' is not.
thinking: Explaining what a hidden group changes
differsFromPlain: Plain practice computes percentages. Here you invent several data sets that satisfy one claim but not another, which shows the gap between 'the most' and 'a majority'.
prerequisites: Can add and compare whole numbers up to 200
Knows 찬성, 반대, 모름, 과반
material: A newspaper polled 200 people about a new policy. Each person answered 찬성 (in favour), 반대 (opposed) or 모름 (not sure). In this task, 과반 means more than half of ALL 200 people asked (so more than 100).

steps.prompt: The poll found 찬성 60, 반대 90, 모름 50. Which headline claims more than these counts support?
hints: For each headline, write down the count or share it needs in order to be true.
Check each of them against 60, 90 and 50 out of 200.

options.text: 새 정책, 반대가 찬성보다 30명 많아
options.reveals: Reading the counts exactly: 90 - 60 = 30.

options.text: 새 정책 반대 응답, 찬성보다 많아
options.reveals: Comparing only the two answers and leaving out the third.

options.text: 국민 과반, 새 정책 반대
options.reveals: Treating 'most' as 'more than any other group' and missing that 90 of 200 is under half.

options.text: 새 정책 반대 45%·찬성 30%·모름 25%
options.reveals: Converting counts into shares of the whole group (90, 60, 50 out of 200).

steps.explain: 과반 means more than half. Half of 200 is 100, and 90 is fewer, so the headline with 과반 overreaches. The others report the counts correctly.

steps.prompt: Enter three different poll results (200 people in total) where opposed is the largest group (more than 찬성 and more than 모름), but not more than 100, with at least 20 in favour and at least 20 answering 모름.
hints: Pick the number opposed first; keep it at 100 or below.
Then choose smaller numbers for in favour and for 모름 so that all three add up to 200.

constraints.expr: floor(a)==a && floor(b)==b && floor(c)==c && a>=0 && b>=0 && c>=0
constraints.fail: Use whole numbers of people, not negative.
The three numbers must add up to 200.
Opposed must be greater than in favour.
Opposition is over half, so it IS a majority.

constraints.ok: Opposed is larger than 모름 too, so it is the largest group.
constraints.fail: Opposed must be larger than 모름, so that it is the largest group.
At least 20 must be in favour.

steps.explain: For example 60/90/50 and 70/100/30 both have more people opposed than in favour, yet opposition is not above 100. 100 is exactly half, which is not 'more than half'.

because.prompt: In English or Korean, explain why 'opposed is the largest group' does not allow the headline '과반 반대', and what role the other two groups play.
hints: Think about how many people did not oppose.
Look at your own examples.

checks.label: mentions majority / half
mentions the not-sure group or the others

selfAssess: Did I use my own numbers?
Did I say who is not counted among the opposed?

modelAnswers.text: 반대가 찬성보다 많아도 100명을 넘지 않으면 과반이 아니에요. 모름이라고 답한 사람이 많으면 반대 비율은 절반 미만이라서 '국민 반대' 헤드라인이 과장일 수 있어요.
More opposed than in favour does not mean a majority: with 90 of 200 opposed, 110 people did not oppose, many answered 모름 or in favour.
Largest group is only a plurality; the 모름 and 찬성 together can be as big as or bigger than 반대.

badAnswers.why: Restates the total; no reasoning about majority or the third group.

because.humanReview: Whether the reasoning distinguishes the largest group from a majority.

rubric.full: Three valid, different result sets
Distinguishes largest group from majority and uses the not-sure group

alternatives: Any triple with a < b <= 100, c >= 20 and sum 200 is valid, e.g. 20/100/80.
A student may also include 모름 above 100 (e.g. 0/50/150); this is valid.
hardCases: A set where 모름 is large but 찬성 is tiny shows the same idea; both are valid.

cautions.language: 과반 means more than half, exactly half is not 과반; the explanation states this.
cautions.culture: The poll is invented and describes no real policy or population.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The counts are given as numbers; enter whole numbers in the three fields.

auto: Choices in s1
Validity of the three result sets and the keywords in the explanation

subject: korean
title: Is 'I'll think about it' a yes?
goal: Decide which information would help read an ambiguous workplace reply and pick a follow-up message that finds out without pressuring or assuming.
differsFromPlain: Plain practice translates '생각해 보겠습니다' as 'I will think about it'. Here you decide what that reply could mean in context and which facts would settle it.
prerequisites: Can read a short workplace chat
Knows -겠습니다 as a polite ending
material: 현우 sent a proposal to 박 부장님 (a department head) by messenger. The reply: "좋은 아이디어네요. 한번 생각해 보겠습니다." 현우 cannot tell if it is a yes, a no or a maybe.

steps.prompt: Which extra pieces of information would help 현우 read the reply? Choose all that apply.
hints: Which facts would a person who is really interested produce, but a person who is declining would not?
Which fact compares this reply with the same person's earlier replies?

options.text: Whether 박 부장님 asked follow-up questions about the budget or schedule
options.reveals: Looking for signs of real interest, which a polite no rarely includes.

options.text: Whether the message was sent in the morning or at night
options.reveals: Using a detail that says little about the answer.

options.text: Whether 박 부장님 usually says this before approving or before declining
options.reveals: Looking for the speaker's own habit, the best key to an indirect reply.

options.text: Whether the reply used -습니다 rather than -어요
options.reveals: Treating the ending as the signal, although endings follow rank, not yes or no.

options.text: Whether the reply came within minutes or only after several days
options.reveals: Using speed as weak evidence of interest.

steps.explain: Follow-up questions (a) and the speaker's habit (c) tell the most about whether the reply is a soft no. Time of day (b) and the ending (d) say little, and reply speed (e) is only weak evidence.

acceptable.reason: Reply speed (e) is weak but reasonable additional evidence.

steps.prompt: Which follow-up message from 현우 best finds out the answer without pressure or assumption?
hints: Imagine you are 박 부장님: which message would you answer most easily?
Check each option for assuming, demanding or pressing.

options.text: 그럼 내일부터 바로 진행하겠습니다. 감사합니다, 부장님.
options.reveals: Assuming a yes and acting on it.

options.text: 그럼 하라는 말씀이신가요, 하지 말라는 말씀이신가요? 확실히 알고 싶습니다.
options.reveals: Asking bluntly and putting the senior on the spot.

options.text: 말씀 감사합니다. 검토에 필요한 자료나 일정이 있으시면 알려 주세요.
options.reveals: Offering help and opening the door to a clear answer without pressure.

options.text: 생각해 보신다고 하셨으니 이번 주 안으로 꼭 답을 주셨으면 합니다.
options.reveals: Setting a deadline, which can feel like pressure on a senior.

steps.explain: Option c keeps the senior's face, offers help and invites more information. a assumes a yes, b is blunt and d pressures.

rubric.full: Picks follow-up questions and the speaker's habit
Chooses a message that offers help and does not assume or press
rubric.partial: Chooses an acceptable but weaker message
rubric.none: Chooses an assuming or pressing message

alternatives: Reply speed (e) is acceptable as extra evidence.
In s2 only c fully matches; d could be acceptable in workplaces with fixed deadlines.
hardCases: In some workplaces '생각해 보겠습니다' simply means the manager will think; the task treats it as ambiguous, not as always a no.

cautions.language: -겠습니다 can mean future or polite resolve; here it is the latter.
cautions.culture: Indirect refusal is common in many cultures; the claim that this phrase 'often means no' is a tendency, not a rule.
cautions.accessibility: No images. Messages are single plain-text lines.

auto: Choices in s1 and s2
human: Open reflection is not included; discuss with a teacher if students disagree

subject: korean
title: Saying no to a 회식
goal: Find the phrase in a reply to a team leader that is inappropriate by itself, then rewrite the whole reply to decline politely.
differsFromPlain: Plain practice drills refusal sentences. Here you evaluate a real draft, find a phrase that is wrong whatever its meaning, and rewrite the message so that the refusal keeps the relationship.
prerequisites: Can write -습니다 sentences
Knows 회식 (a team dinner), 선약, 공지
material: The team leader posted in the group chat: "이번 금요일 6시 팀 회식입니다. 다들 참석 바랍니다." A new employee has a family appointment that evening. Their draft reply:

steps.prompt: One phrase in the draft is a well-known problem when speaking to a superior, whatever the refusal is. Which line contains it?
hints: Ask of each line: would it be a problem if said to a superior in ANY message, apart from the refusal?
Separate lines that are only blunt in this situation from a phrase that is wrong whatever the message is.
steps.explain: Line 4 is the problem. 수고하세요 is said to someone of equal or lower rank; to a superior many Koreans prefer 먼저 가보겠습니다 or 고생하셨습니다. Line 2 is also blunt (못 가요), but that can be fixed by wording the refusal more softly; 수고하세요 is wrong whatever the refusal says.

steps.prompt: Rewrite the reply in Korean (2-4 sentences): acknowledge the notice, decline politely with a reason, and show goodwill.
hints: Thank or acknowledge first, then apologise before the refusal.
Replace '못 가요' with a softer expression of difficulty.

checks.label: acknowledges the notice
apologises or shows regret
shows goodwill or an alternative
avoids the blunt phrases from the draft
gives a reason
declines (says that attending is difficult / not possible)

selfAssess: Does the refusal come with respect and a reason?
Did I avoid ending with 수고하세요?
Does it sound like someone who still values the team?

modelAnswers.text: 팀장님, 회식 공지 확인했습니다. 죄송하지만 그날은 가족과의 선약이 있어 참석하기 어려울 것 같습니다. 다음 회식에는 꼭 참석하겠습니다. 즐거운 시간 보내시기 바랍니다.
팀장님, 알려 주셔서 감사합니다. 이번 금요일에는 선약이 있어 함께하지 못해 아쉽습니다. 양해 부탁드립니다. 다음에는 꼭 함께하겠습니다.

badAnswers.text: 팀장님, 금요일 회식 공지 확인했습니다. 그날은 선약이 있어서 못 가요. 다음에는 꼭 참석하고 싶습니다. 그럼 수고하세요.
badAnswers.why: The original draft: blunt and ends with an inappropriate phrase.
Blunt, no acknowledgement, no apology.

badAnswers.text: 팀장님, 공지 확인했습니다. 죄송합니다. 다음에 참석하겠습니다.
badAnswers.why: Polite, but gives no reason and never says that the writer cannot come on Friday.

steps.humanReview: Naturalness and whether the tone is neither servile nor curt.

rubric.full: Identifies 수고하세요 and says why
rubric.partial: Identifies a line without a reason

rubric.full: Acknowledges, apologises, gives a reason and shows goodwill

alternatives: Declining with a vague reason ('개인 사정이 있어서') is acceptable.
A reply offering to join for the first hour is also a valid choice.
hardCases: Acceptance of 수고하세요 to superiors varies by person and workplace; the task treats it as a common source of offence, not a universal rule.

cautions.language: 수고하세요 and 수고하셨습니다 to superiors are debated; the task uses the more cautious norm.
cautions.culture: Expectations about attending a 회식 vary; many companies make it voluntary. The task does not say that skipping is wrong.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The group chat is plain text.

auto: The problem line in s1
Acknowledgement, apology, goodwill and avoidance of blunt phrases in s2

subject: korean
title: Write a sentence that explains the idiom
goal: Choose the sentence whose context teaches an idiom, then write your own sentence for an idiom and name its clue and its possible misreading.
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks for an idiom's meaning. Here you make the context that lets a reader infer it, and you identify the clue and the misreading risk yourself.
prerequisites: Knows the three idioms from the glosses
Can write a two-clause Korean sentence
material: Idioms: 귀가 얇다 (to be easily swayed by what others say), 입이 무겁다 (to keep secrets), 눈이 높다 (to have high standards, to be picky). A good example sentence lets a reader infer the meaning from the situation.

steps.prompt: Which sentence best lets a reader infer the meaning of 귀가 얇다 without a gloss?
hints: Cover the idiom and ask what a reader could still learn about 민지.
Eliminate sentences that would be true if she simply had thin ears.

options.text: 민지는 어릴 때부터 친구가 많고 늘 웃는 얼굴인데 귀가 얇아요.
options.reveals: Adding facts that do not bear on the idiom, so the reader cannot infer anything.

options.text: 다들 알다시피 민지는 정말로 귀가 얇은 사람이라서 그 점이 늘 화제예요.
options.reveals: Repeating the idiom with no situation; it explains nothing.

options.text: 민지는 귀가 얇아서 광고에 끌려 사고 친구가 말리면 금방 마음을 바꿔요.
options.reveals: Giving behaviours that show being swayed, and a reason clause that links them.

options.text: 민지는 귀가 얇아서 겨울에 귀마개 없이는 금방 귀가 빨개져요.
options.reveals: Making a context that supports a literal reading of ears.

steps.explain: Option c gives behaviour (buying because of an ad, changing mind when friends object) that reveals the meaning. a adds irrelevant detail, b is circular, and d supports the literal reading.

steps.prompt: Choose ONE of the three idioms and write two Korean sentences so that a reader who has never seen it can infer its meaning from the situation.
hints: Show what the person does or what happens, not a definition.
Connect the situation to the idiom with a reason clause.

checks.label: uses one of the idioms
gives a reason, contrast or result
shows a behaviour or situation that fits the meaning of the idiom

selfAssess: Would the reader guess the meaning if the idiom were hidden?
Could my sentences also fit a literal reading?

modelAnswers.text: 수지는 입이 무거워서 내가 말해 준 비밀을 아무에게도 얘기하지 않았다. 그래서 나는 고민이 생기면 수지에게 제일 먼저 말한다.
그 사람은 눈이 높아서 소개팅을 열 번 해도 마음에 드는 사람이 없대요. 외모뿐 아니라 성격이나 직업도 까다롭게 따지거든요.
그는 입이 무거워서 내가 말한 비밀을 아무에게도 말하지 않았어요.

badAnswers.why: The idiom alone; no situation or clue.
Does not use any of the idioms.
Uses the idiom and a connective, but nothing in the situation shows what 귀가 얇다 means.

steps.humanReview: Whether the situation really reveals the meaning and the Korean is natural.

steps.prompt: In English, name the exact Korean words in your sentences that give the meaning away, and say how a reader could still misread the idiom (for example literally).
hints: Quote the clause that carries the clue.
Think of the literal meaning of the body part.

checks.label: quotes a Korean phrase (two or more words)
names a possible misreading

selfAssess: Did I quote, not paraphrase?
Is my misreading a real alternative?
Is the phrase I quoted really in my own sentences?

modelAnswers.text: The clue is 아무에게도 얘기하지 않았다; a reader could still take 입이 무겁다 literally as a heavy mouth, but the secret context makes that unlikely.
눈이 높아서 + 마음에 드는 사람이 없대요 are the clues. Someone might misread 눈 as eyesight, but the dating context makes the standards reading clear.

badAnswers.why: No quoted words and no misreading.

steps.humanReview: Whether the identified clue is the real one.

rubric.full: Situation reveals the meaning and a reason clause links it
Quotes the clue and names a realistic misreading

alternatives: Any of the three idioms is acceptable; sentences about oneself or about a character are both fine.
A longer story with three sentences is also fine.
hardCases: A sentence may reveal meaning only through a gloss ('귀가 얇다, 즉 ...'); treat as weaker, since the aim is inference.

cautions.language: The glosses are given in English; the task aims at creating context, not at recalling them.
cautions.culture: Idioms with body parts exist in many languages, but their meanings differ; the task warns about literal readings.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The checker looks for two or more Hangul characters in s3 and does not judge quality.

auto: Choice in s1
Idiom use, connectors and quoted Korean in s2 and s3
human: Whether the clues truly reveal the idiom
